eligibility: eligible (pre-registered in unstated/protocol/targets.py before any audit past rank 10) — hook call order and the firstresult rule depend on properties of the plugins the caller registers

hypotheses.statement: With firstresult=True, every hookimpl but one has its return value silently discarded. Nothing tells the caller another plugin also answered.
Hook call order is LIFO in registration, so a plugin registered LATER takes precedence. Precedence is therefore decided by import order, an environment property the caller never stated.
tryfirst/trylast do not impose a total order. Two impls carrying the same marker fall back to registration order, so 'I marked mine tryfirst' does not guarantee it runs first.
An exception raised in one hookimpl aborts the whole hook call, so contributions from impls that had not yet run are lost, and the caller cannot tell a partial result from a complete one.

measurements.what: two plugins answer a firstresult hook
measurements.result: both produced values [80, 100]; the hook returned 80 and discarded 100; 0 warnings, 0 exceptions
the same two plugins return 100 instead of 80 — LIFO, the last registered runs first
2 of 2 registration orders produced a different winner: A-then-B returns 'B', B-then-A returns 'A'. The marker does not break the tie.

measurements.what: can the discarded answers be recovered
measurements.result: no: the return value is a bare int, get_hookimpls() lists 2 implementations but no values, and add_hookcall_monitoring reports only [('resolve', 80)]
17 of 52 pytest hookspecs (33%) are firstresult=True, including pytest_fixture_setup and pytest_ignore_collect
a plugin returning None falls through (result 100); a plugin returning 0 wins (result 0), so None can never be a legitimate answer
raises ValueError to the caller; the working plugin's answer of 100 is not returned. LOUD, not a finding.

measurements.what: instrumented both impls to record entry
measurements.result: registering catalogue,promotion gives value=80 and implementations_that_ran=['promotion'] — 1 of 2. The loser's body never executes.
all-plain A,B,C -> C,B,A; all-tryfirst A,B,C -> C,B,A; all-trylast A,B,C -> A,B,C. 1 of 3 marker classes is FIFO, so LIFO is not the rule.

measurements.what: does any API expose the contention
measurements.result: 3 of 3 do: get_hookimpls()+spec.opts identifies it, add_hookcall_monitoring passes the full 2-impl list to both callbacks, subset_hook_caller(remove_plugins=[winner]) returns 100 — the loser's answer.
9 of 17 first-result hookspecs already have >1 answering implementation with 0 third-party plugins; 17 of 52 hookspecs are firstresult (16 of 52 at pytest 7.4.4).

measurements.what: does one unrelated plugin change the decider
measurements.result: yes — registering pytest-subtests changed the deciding implementation on 3 of 3 hooks it joined, 0 warnings. A first probe using pytest-timeout/xdist/cov showed 0 of 3, but xdist and cov never loaded — that was a broken probe, not a negative.
the test is `is not None`: [None,0] returns 0, [None,False] returns False, [None,''] returns '', each running 1 of 2 impls; [None,None] returns None having run 2 of 2.

hypothesis_outcomes.evidence: only 1 of 2 impls ran; nothing is discarded because nothing else is computed
all-trylast runs FIFO (A,B,C); LIFO holds within a bucket only
2 of 2 orderings flipped the winner with both impls marked tryfirst

verifier.reason: Central phenomenon real and broader than claimed, but the stated MECHANISM is wrong, the ordering rule is wrong, two 'no API exists' claims are false, one release date is wrong, and the check fires HIGH on stock pytest with zero third-party plugins.
verifier.corrected_claim: pluggy firstresult: when more than one registered plugin can answer, the hook returns the answer of whichever impl pluggy reaches first and NEVER CALLS THE OTHERS — they do not run, so their answers are not computed and their side effects do not occur. Order is decided by pluggy's six buckets (tryfirst -> plain -> trylast, wrappers first within each), and WITHIN a bucket by registration order: later-registered wins among tryfirst and plain, EARLIER-registered wins among trylast. Measured at all 17 releases 0.6.0 (2017-11-24) through 1.6.0 (2025-05-15), 7.5 years, exhaustive over the span, and also at 0.3.0 and 0.4.0 — so 0.6.0 is the earliest measured, not the onset. The value carries no provenance and nothing warns at call time, but it CAN be investigated after the fact: get_hookimpls() + spec.opts identifies a contested hook, add_hookcall_monitoring passes the full impl list to before and after, and subset_hook_caller(name, remove_plugins=[winner]) returns the loser's answer.

proposed_entry.versions_measured: all 17 releases from 0.6.0 through 1.6.0, plus 0.3.0 and 0.4.0
proposed_entry.affected_versions: order-dependent at all 17 releases from 0.6.0 (2017-11-24) through 1.6.0 (2025-05-15, current latest) — 7.5 years, exhaustive over the span. 0.6.0 is the earliest measured, not the onset: 0.3.0 (2015-05-07) and 0.4.0 reproduce identically, and 0.5.0-0.5.2 cannot run on Python 3.11 so are untestable rather than unaffected
proposed_entry.resolved_in: not resolved — documented and by design; tryfirst/trylast exist to influence the order but do not break ties
proposed_entry.assumption: the caller knows which registered plugin answers a first-result hook, and that the others were considered
proposed_entry.cost_when_violated: With two plugins able to answer the same firstresult hook, the value returned flips from 80 to 100 purely by reversing registration order, with 0 warnings and 0 exceptions at all 17 releases across 7.5 years. Only ONE implementation ever runs — _multicall breaks at the first non-None — so the losers' answers are never computed and their side effects never happen. Order is decided by six buckets (tryfirst > plain > trylast, wrappers first within each) and by registration order WITHIN a bucket only: trylast runs FIFO, the opposite of the rest. Two implementations both marked tryfirst still flip with order, 2 of 2 orderings. Contested hooks are normal — 9 of 17 first-result hookspecs on stock pytest 9.1.1 have more than one answering implementation, and 17 of 52 hookspecs are firstresult (16 of 52 at pytest 7.4.4). Registering one unrelated third-party plugin (pytest-subtests) changed the deciding implementation on 3 of 3 hooks it joined, 0 warnings.
proposed_entry.upstream_status: documented and by design; the bucket order is stated in pluggy's own source. The gap is that a contested hook looks exactly like an uncontested one at the point the value is used. The contention is recoverable afterwards via get_hookimpls(), add_hookcall_monitoring and subset_hook_caller — nothing prompts anyone to ask.

impact.believed_claim: My plugin decides this, and the others were considered.
impact.actual_claim: One implementation decides it and the rest never run. Which one is decided by bucket order, then registration order within a bucket — a property of what happens to be installed. Measured: the value flips 80 to 100 by reversing registration, and one unrelated third-party plugin changed the decider on 3 of 3 hooks it joined.
impact.breaks: Whatever the hook decides, differently per installation — and the losers' SIDE EFFECTS do not happen either. A plugin architecture exists so behaviour can be extended: a price resolved, a route chosen, a record classified. When two extensions can both answer, one is never invoked at all, so a plugin that was also supposed to log, count or cache as a side effect of answering silently does none of it. The same application, same code, same inputs behaves differently on a machine where one extra plugin is installed, and the returned value carries nothing saying who produced it.
impact.detection: Poor at the point of use, recoverable afterwards. No exception, no warning, and the value has no provenance. It is not undiscoverable — get_hookimpls(), add_hookcall_monitoring and subset_hook_caller all expose the contention — but nothing prompts anyone to ask, and a contested hook is indistinguishable from an uncontested one until someone does.

verifier_round_2.corrected_claim: pluggy firstresult returns the first non-None answer and never calls the rest; order is set by six buckets (ALL WRAPPERS ahead of ALL non-wrappers, then tryfirst > plain > trylast) and within a bucket by registration order. Two plugins that both answer flip 80<->100 by registration order at every release testable on Python 3.11, 0.3.0 (2015-05-07) through 1.6.0 (2025-05-15); 0.6.0-1.6.0 is all 17 PyPI releases of that span, one of them (1.1.0) yanked. A WRAPPER CAN ALSO DECIDE THE VALUE, by returning one or via force_result, and two competing wrappers flip the same way. NOT supported: that this normally displaces anyone — contested first-result hooks are the ordinary state and in 42 of 42 real calls an earlier impl ran and abstained.
